controllingAuthority.summary: On a showing that the person is a victim of identity theft and was wrongly identified in arrest records or public records, the court must order expungement of the arrest records and public records and must cause the order to be delivered to the relevant law enforcement agencies and courts. Use of Form 4-951 NMRA is mandatory under Rule 1-077.1(D) and (M). Service is not required for this track under Rule 1-077.1(E), and Rule 1-077.1(J) permits the court to decide on the pleadings where no objection is filed.

exclusions: New Mexico district courts cannot expunge records of another state or federal records.

tracks.legalName: Petition to Expunge Arrest Records and Public Records upon Release Without Conviction, NMSA 1978 § 29-3A-4
tracks.publicName: Expunge a New Mexico case that did not end in a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: On petition, where the court finds that no other charge or proceeding is pending and that the person was released without conviction, it must order expungement of the arrest records and public records. 'Released without conviction' is broad: acquittal or a finding of not guilty; nolle prosequi, no bill or other dismissal; referral to a preprosecution diversion programme; an order of conditional discharge under § 31-20-13; or proceedings otherwise discharged. The petition is filed under seal under Rule 1-079 NMRA.

exclusions: Any other charge or proceeding pending anywhere defeats the required finding.
New Mexico district courts cannot expunge records of another state or federal records.

The statutory definition of 'arrest records' excludes DWI citations maintained by the Taxation and Revenue Department, computer-aided dispatch information, and breath alcohol testing equipment log books, so some DWI-related records survive even a successful expungement.

The § 29-3A-2 definitions carve several categories out of 'public records', including confidential arrest-record information, district attorney and attorney general law-enforcement files, certain CYFD, HSD and PED records, and records received through an authorized background check.

controllingAuthority.summary: On petition, after completion of the sentence and payment of any fines or fees owed to the state for that conviction, the court may expunge a conviction of a municipal ordinance violation, misdemeanor or felony. Relief is discretionary: the court must find no other charge or proceeding pending anywhere, that justice will be served, that victim restitution ordered in connection with the conviction has been fulfilled, and that there was no other criminal conviction during the applicable waiting period. Rule 1-077.1(J) requires a hearing; there is no paper-only route.

exclusions: An offense committed against a child.
An offense that caused great bodily harm or death.
A sex offense as defined in NMSA 1978 § 29-11A-3.
Embezzlement under NMSA 1978 § 30-16-8.
An offense involving driving while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or drugs.
Any other criminal conviction during the applicable waiting period.
Any other charge or proceeding pending anywhere.
Unfulfilled victim restitution ordered in connection with the conviction.
New Mexico district courts cannot expunge records of another state or federal records.

units.description: Every conviction petition ends at a hearing: Rule 1-077.1(J) requires the court to hold one to determine whether the § 29-3A-5(C) requirements are met. Guidance covers what the hearing decides, that the burden is on the petitioner, that the justice-will-be-served narrative is argument LegalEase does not write, that the court issues its order within sixty days, and that the expungement then takes at least another sixty days to complete.

destination.detail: Civil petition, not sealed. Served on the district attorney for the county where the conviction was entered, the New Mexico Department of Public Safety, and the law enforcement agency that arrested the petitioner. Those parties have sixty days to object on Form 4-957 or to file a non-objection on Form 4-958. A hearing is mandatory. The court issues its order within sixty days of the hearing, any order must allow a minimum of sixty days to complete the expungement, court records may not be expunged earlier than thirty days from entry of the order, and any order granting a petition must require that the civil expungement proceeding itself be expunged. Denial may be appealed to the Court of Appeals.

controllingAuthority.summary: Where a person was charged with an offence involving cannabis that is no longer a crime as of June 29, 2021, or that would have resulted in a lesser offence had the Cannabis Regulation Act been in effect, then whether or not there was a conviction, all public records held by a court or a state or local agency relating to the arrest or conviction are automatically expunged two years after the conviction date, or two years after the arrest date if there was no conviction. For minors the record is retained for two years or until the person turns eighteen, whichever comes first. Automatic expungement applies to records involving only cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges and requires destruction of the records. The 2023 amendment requires the Administrative Office of the Courts to implement a verification procedure and an administrative request route for mixed cases, and Rule 1-077.1(B)(4) provides that there is no filing fee for an action commenced under § 29-3A-8.

exclusions: Records involving anything other than cannabis and cannabis paraphernalia charges. Only the portion of the records related to the cannabis charges is expunged under § 29-3A-8.

Anyone currently or formerly incarcerated for a cannabis offence, who belongs in the sentence dismissal and vacatur track.
